title: America's Nuclear Industry Just Landed in India With a $100 Billion Question. The Answer Could Reshape Both Countries' Energy Futures.
excerpt: A 20-member US delegation is in New Delhi and Mumbai this week to explore what India's newly opened nuclear sector means for American companies — and for a country that needs 100 GW of clean power by 2047.
body:
On Sunday, a 20-member delegation of senior American nuclear industry executives arrived in New Delhi. By the time they leave Mumbai on Wednesday, they will have met India's Finance Minister, its Minister of State for Science and Technology, officials from the Department of Atomic Energy, and a constellation of private-sector stakeholders. The agenda: what it will take to build a nuclear partnership worth tens of billions of dollars.

The visit, organised jointly by the Nuclear Energy Institute and the US-India Strategic Partnership Forum, is the most significant American engagement with India's nuclear sector since the landmark 2008 civil nuclear deal. And unlike that earlier moment — which was defined by geopolitical symbolism — this one is driven by hard commercial logic.

## India Opens the Door

The backdrop to this week's meetings is a regulatory transformation that would have seemed unthinkable a decade ago. In 2025, India enacted the SHANTI Act — the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India — which for the first time allows private-sector participation in the country's nuclear energy programme. Foreign Direct Investment of up to 49 per cent is now permitted in nuclear power projects.

For American companies that have spent years watching India's nuclear ambitions from the sidelines, blocked by liability disputes and bureaucratic caution, the door is now open.

"Technology collaborations and strategic partnerships can serve as critical drivers of innovation and resilience in India's nuclear ecosystem," Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman told the delegation on Tuesday, urging them to "actively explore opportunities for engagement and long-term collaboration."

## The Scale of the Opportunity

India's nuclear ambitions are staggering in scope. The country currently operates 8.8 GW of nuclear capacity. Under the Viksit Bharat 2047 vision, it aims to reach 100 GW — a more than tenfold increase in just over two decades.

The near-term milestones are already being set. India has allocated nearly ₹20,000 crore (roughly $2.4 billion) for five Small Modular Reactors by 2033. The proposed Westinghouse AP1000 project at Kovvada in Andhra Pradesh, long stalled by liability concerns, is back on the table. And India achieved a quiet but historic milestone on April 6, when its indigenously designed 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam achieved first criticality — making India only the second country after Russia to operate a commercial-level fast breeder reactor.

Minister of State Dr Jitendra Singh told the delegation that collaboration extends well beyond reactors. He outlined opportunities in micro-reactors, AI-enabled nuclear safety systems, scientific computing, rare earth processing, and the LIGO-India gravitational wave observatory — a ₹2,600 crore project being built in partnership with American institutions.

## Why America Needs This Too

The visit is not just about India's needs. America's nuclear industry has been in a decades-long decline, with few new reactors built and an ageing fleet struggling to compete with cheap natural gas and renewables. A market as large as India's — with its government commitment, regulatory reforms, and sheer electricity demand — offers American nuclear firms something they desperately need: a growth story.

The TRUST Initiative, launched during Prime Minister Modi's meeting with President Trump in February 2025, provides the diplomatic framework. Centred on trusted technology partnerships, resilient supply chains, and innovation ecosystems, it covers artificial intelligence, semiconductors, biotechnology, quantum technologies, and — critically — nuclear energy.

## The Diaspora Bridge

For Indian-American professionals working in America's nuclear and energy sectors, this partnership creates a unique position. Many of the engineers, physicists, and policy experts who staff US national laboratories, nuclear utilities, and regulatory agencies are of Indian origin. As the two countries build a commercial nuclear corridor, these professionals become natural intermediaries — carrying technical expertise, cultural fluency, and professional networks that span both sides.

The SHANTI Act's FDI provisions also open investment pathways for NRIs. Nuclear energy infrastructure — reactor construction, fuel fabrication, spent fuel management, advanced materials — requires the kind of long-term capital that diaspora investors and institutions have increasingly sought to deploy in India.

## The Obstacles Remain Real

For all the optimism, the path is not without obstacles. The nuclear liability law that nearly torpedoed the original civil nuclear deal remains on the books, though its practical impact has been softened by administrative measures. Land acquisition for new reactor sites is perennially contentious. And India's nuclear establishment — long dominated by the state — will need to develop a regulatory culture that accommodates private players without compromising safety.

The Westinghouse Kovvada project, in particular, will be a bellwether. If it moves from memorandum of understanding to concrete and steel, it will signal that the partnership has moved beyond rhetoric. If it stalls again, the credibility of the entire framework will be questioned.

## What This Week Decides

The American delegation's four-day visit will not produce a signed contract or a headline-grabbing deal. What it will produce — if the conversations go well — is a shared understanding of where the commercial seams are: which technologies India needs, which American companies can supply them, and what the regulatory and financial architecture must look like to make it work.

For India, the stakes are existential. A country that will soon be the world's most populous cannot meet its climate commitments or its development aspirations without a massive expansion of clean baseload power. For America, the stakes are strategic: a nuclear partnership with India is a hedge against Chinese dominance in the global nuclear supply chain.

And for the diaspora, watching from both sides of the Pacific, it is one more thread in the increasingly dense web that connects the world's oldest democracy to its largest.
